sections.heading: La francophonie
sections.body: About 320 million people speak French across five continents. *La francophonie* (lower case) is the French-speaking world; *l'Organisation internationale de la Francophonie* (OIF) is the institution. This course teaches metropolitan French, but at C1 you should **recognise** the main varieties — and know that none is "wrong".

sections.heading: Belgium and Switzerland
sections.body:
- numbers: *septante* (70), *nonante* (90) in Belgium and Switzerland; in some Swiss cantons also *huitante* (80). *Quatre-vingt-dix-sept* in Paris, *nonante-sept* in Brussels.
- meals: *le déjeuner* (breakfast), *le dîner* (lunch), *le souper* (dinner) — as in Québec.
- Belgium: *une fois* used as a filler (*Viens ici une fois*), *un GSM* (a mobile phone), *une drache* (a downpour).
- Switzerland: *un natel* (a mobile phone), *septante*, *nonante*, slower rhythm.

sections.heading: Québec
sections.body:
Québécois French has its own pronunciation (*t* and *d* before the vowels of *tu* and *dit* gain a hiss: /tsy/, /dzi/), vocabulary and expressions, and strongly resists anglicisms in official usage:
- *le courriel* (email) — *la fin de semaine* (the weekend) — *magasiner* (to go shopping) — *un char* (a car, familiar) — *un dépanneur* (a corner shop) — *ma blonde* (my girlfriend), *mon chum* (my boyfriend; a mate) — *C'est plate.* (It's boring.) — *Il fait frette.* (It's freezing.)
- *Bienvenue !* also means "You're welcome" (from English).

sections.heading: Africa
sections.body: French is an official language in some twenty African countries, and Africa is home to most of the world's francophones. Local words enrich it: *un maquis* (an open-air eatery, Côte d'Ivoire), *un taxi-brousse* (a bush taxi), *une essencerie* (a petrol station, Senegal), *ambiancer* (to liven up a party), *un deuxième bureau* (a mistress — literally a second office). Many speakers are multilingual, mixing French with Wolof, Lingala, Bambara and others.

examples: Le français est parlé sur cinq continents.
French is spoken on five continents.
La plupart des francophones vivent en Afrique.
Most French speakers live in Africa.
À Bruxelles, on dit « septante » et « nonante ».
In Brussels, people say "septante" and "nonante".
En Belgique, le dîner est le repas de midi.
In Belgium, "dîner" is the midday meal.
Au Québec, on dit « courriel » plutôt que « mail ».
In Québec, people say "courriel" rather than "mail".
Qu'est-ce que tu fais en fin de semaine ?
What are you doing at the weekend?
Elle est partie magasiner au centre-ville.
She went shopping downtown.
Je vais au dépanneur acheter du lait.
I'm going to the corner shop to buy milk.
Le Québec lutte contre les anglicismes.
Québec fights against anglicisms.
On a mangé dans un maquis à Abidjan.
We ate at an open-air eatery in Abidjan.
Beaucoup d'Africains sont multilingues.
Many Africans are multilingual.
Aucune variété du français n'est « fausse ».
No variety of French is "wrong".
